Fragment-size distribution in cM — theory and cross-caller validation

Author

Fausto Rodríguez-Zapata

Published

June 26, 2026

Repo: sawers-rellan-labs/zealtiger

The introgression-size panel compares the five callers (Skim-RTI / BrB-RTI / Skim-BIN / Skim-nilHMM / BrB-nilHMM) against the n=1500 BC2S3 simulation in megabases. The Mb fragment-size law has no closed form: it is the genetic-distance (cM) law pushed through the cM→Mb change of variables \(x_{\text{Mb}}=\int dx_{\text{cM}}/\rho(x)\), and the local recombination rate \(\rho(x)=d\text{cM}/d\text{Mb}\) is an empirical, position-dependent lookup (strong pericentromeric suppression, hot arms) — so the simulation is doing Monte-Carlo integration over the map. In cM the segment-length law is analytic. This document

  1. derives the theoretical donor-segment-size distribution in cM from the BC2S3 recombination model,
  2. confirms the derived law reproduces the simcross output (its own cM segment lengths), and
  3. uses it as a map-free reference to validate the five callers, after converting their called Mb segments back to cM through the consensus map.

Why this is a validation panel, not the calibration metric. A caller’s resolution limit lives in Mb (Skim-BIN’s hard 1 Mb floor; RTIGER’s marker-space rigidity r). Converting to cM turns a clean Mb floor into a position-dependent cM floor (≈0 cM at a centromere, tens of cM on an arm), entangling caller resolution with map non-linearity. So the Mb panel stays the r-calibration space; this cM panel tests whether the population’s fragment law matches the analytic recombination expectation, with the map entering once, deterministically, on the data side. It leans on conserved marker order relative to the consensus map — load-bearing here, since any introgression with local rearrangement makes \(\rho(x)\) wrong and biases \(\Delta\)cM.

Part 1 — The theoretical fragment-size distribution in cM

The crossover process (Haldane)

Under Haldane’s no-interference model, crossovers along a chromosome form a homogeneous Poisson process in genetic distance: 1 Morgan = 1 expected crossover, and the count in any interval of length \(\ell\) Morgans is \(\text{Poisson}(\ell)\). Consequently the distance to the next crossover is exponential,

\[P(D > x) = e^{-x}, \qquad x \text{ in Morgans},\]

with mean 1 Morgan, \(\text{CV}=1\), skewness \(=2\) — the most-skewed member of the gamma family (\(\text{Gamma}(1)\)). Genetic distance is literally the scale parameter: it is the expected number of crossovers, so it plays the role temperature plays for a Maxwell–Boltzmann speed.

From crossovers to junctions: superposition over meioses

A donor↔︎recurrent boundary (“junction”) on the final NIL haplotype is a crossover — laid down in some meiosis of the NIL’s ancestry — that happened to fall where one parental haplotype carried donor ancestry and the other recurrent. If the NIL haplotype descends through \(g\) meioses since the donor haplotype was intact, and each meiosis sprinkles an independent Poisson(\(1/\)Morgan) crossover field, the superposition of those \(g\) fields is itself Poisson at rate \(g\) per Morgan. (Exact under Haldane; and by the Palm–Khinchin superposition theorem, the pooled process tends to Poisson even with per-meiosis interference, because independent point processes superpose toward Poisson.)

If every crossover were a junction, junction density would be \(g\)/Morgan and donor tracts would be \(\text{Exp}(g)\). The correction is that only crossovers in still-heterozygous (donor/recurrent) territory create a D↔︎R junction, and that territory shrinks each generation as the donor fraction is diluted. So the effective junction rate is \(\lambda \le g\).

Counting meioses in the BC2S3 pedigree

The simulated scheme (R/02_simulate.R, bc2s3_pedigree()) is two backcrosses to the recurrent parent then three generations of selfing; the donor founder (id 2) is inbred, so the donor haplotype enters the F1 (id 3) intact and is first broken in the F1’s meiosis. Tracing one homolog of the final NIL (id 8) back to that intact donor haplotype crosses five meioses:

# meiosis (gametogenesis in) produces territory still D/R
1 F1 (id 3) BC1 (id 4) whole genome (F1 het everywhere)
2 BC1 (id 4) BC2 (id 5) donor regions only (~50% of remaining)
3 BC2 (id 5) S1 (id 6) shrinking donor regions
4 S1 (id 6) S2 (id 7) shrinking donor regions
5 S2 (id 7) S3 (id 8) = NIL shrinking donor regions

So \(g = 5\). The naïve Haldane prediction is therefore \(\text{Exp}(5)\) per Morgan — donor tracts with mean \(1/5\) Morgan \(= 20\) cM. Because junction-creating territory shrinks after meiosis 1, the effective rate is a bit below 5.

The donor-tract length distribution

Two quantities, distinguished by the inspection paradox:

  • Genome-wide tracts (a randomly chosen donor segment, no selection): by renewal theory the length is \(\text{Exp}(\lambda)\), mean \(1/\lambda\) Morgans.
  • The tract covering a fixed target locus (a selected NIL around a target gene): length-biased → left flank + right flank, each \(\text{Exp}(\lambda)\), so \(T^\star \sim \text{Gamma}(2,\lambda)\), mean \(2/\lambda\), skewness \(\sqrt2\approx1.41\). This is the \(\text{Gamma}(2)\) “segment around a locus” case.

These simulations are unselected, so the genome-wide quantity applies — the law sits near the exponential end, not at \(\text{Gamma}(2)\).

Three departures from the clean exponential

The simulated segments are not exactly \(\text{Exp}(5)\) for three reasons, each pushing in a definite direction:

  1. Union of the two haplotypes. A simulated “segment” is the union of donor intervals across the mat and pat homologs (a region is introgressed if either carries donor). Unions merge nearby tracts and lengthen them → mean up, and the shortest tracts are absorbed → shape \(k>1\).
  2. Interference (\(m=10\)). simcross uses the Stahl chi-square model with \(m=10,\,p=0\) (a crossover at every 11th point of a Poisson process) — strong positive interference, which regularizes spacing within each meiosis → \(\text{CV}<1\), skewness \(<2\), again \(k>1\).
  3. Shrinking heterozygous territory. Only meiosis 1 acts genome-wide; later meioses add junctions only in the dwindling donor neighborhoods → effective rate \(\lambda<g=5\).

The theoretical distribution we will test against

Net: the donor-tract length in cM is well-described by a gamma law

\[T \sim \text{Gamma}(k,\lambda), \qquad k \gtrsim 1,\ \lambda \lesssim 5\ \text{Morgan}^{-1},\]

bracketed below by \(\text{Exp}(5)\) (no interference, no union, full rate) and above by \(\text{Gamma}(2)\) (the locus-anchored / heavily size-biased extreme). Part 2 estimates \((k,\lambda)\) from the simulation and checks both brackets; Part 3 uses the fitted analytic law plus the simulation’s own cM lengths as the reference for the callers.

Code 
library(tidyverse)
theme_set(theme_bw())

nil_seg <- read_csv(params$nil_seg, show_col_types = FALSE)
# simulated segments carry BOTH endpoints; the cM length is exact (no map needed) — this IS the
# generative model's realization of the law derived above.
sim_cm <- nil_seg %>% transmute(cm = end_cm - start_cm, M = (end_cm - start_cm) / 100)

g  <- 5                                   # meioses on the donor lineage (pedigree count)
mu <- mean(sim_cm$cm)                     # empirical mean (cM)

cat(sprintf("sim cM segments: n=%d | mean %.2f  median %.2f  sd %.2f  CV %.3f  skew %.3f\n",
            nrow(sim_cm), mu, median(sim_cm$cm), sd(sim_cm$cm),
            sd(sim_cm$cm)/mu, mean(((sim_cm$cm - mu)/sd(sim_cm$cm))^3)))
sim cM segments: n=15523 | mean 24.29  median 18.92  sd 21.33  CV 0.878  skew 1.574

Part 2 — Does the derived law reproduce the simulation?

We fit \(\text{Gamma}(k,\lambda)\) to the simulation’s own cM segment lengths by maximum likelihood, and overlay the two analytic brackets, \(\text{Exp}(5)\) and the mean-matched \(\text{Gamma}(2)\).

Code 
fit <- MASS::fitdistr(sim_cm$M, "gamma")           # in Morgans
k   <- unname(fit$estimate["shape"])
lam <- unname(fit$estimate["rate"])                # per Morgan
ks_gamma <- suppressWarnings(ks.test(sim_cm$M, "pgamma", shape = k, rate = lam)$statistic)
ks_exp5  <- suppressWarnings(ks.test(sim_cm$M, "pexp",  rate = g)$statistic)
ks_gam2  <- suppressWarnings(ks.test(sim_cm$M, "pgamma", shape = 2, rate = 2/mean(sim_cm$M))$statistic)

cat(sprintf("Gamma MLE (cM): shape k=%.3f  rate lambda=%.3f /Morgan  -> mean %.2f cM, CV %.3f, skew %.3f\n",
            k, lam, 100*k/lam, 1/sqrt(k), 2/sqrt(k)))
Gamma MLE (cM): shape k=1.146  rate lambda=4.716 /Morgan  -> mean 24.29 cM, CV 0.934, skew 1.869
Code 
cat(sprintf("KS vs derived Gamma(k,lambda): D=%.4f   [Exp(5): D=%.4f | Gamma(2): D=%.4f]\n",
            ks_gamma, ks_exp5, ks_gam2))
KS vs derived Gamma(k,lambda): D=0.0281   [Exp(5): D=0.1135 | Gamma(2): D=0.1059]

The fitted \(k\approx1.15\), \(\lambda\approx4.72\)/Morgan lands exactly where the derivation predicts: just above the exponential (\(k>1\), from interference + the union) with a rate a little under \(g=5\) (shrinking het territory). It fits the simulation tightly (KS \(D\approx0.028\)), while both brackets — \(\text{Exp}(5)\) and \(\text{Gamma}(2)\) — are rejected, confirming the segment law sits between them, near the exponential end.

Code 
xs <- seq(0, quantile(sim_cm$cm, 0.995), length.out = 400)
curves <- bind_rows(
  tibble(cm = xs, d = dgamma(xs/100, shape = k, rate = lam)/100,
         curve = sprintf("BC2S3 expectation: Gamma(k=%.2f, λ=%.1f)", k, lam)),
  tibble(cm = xs, d = dexp(xs/100, rate = g)/100,           curve = "Exp(5)  [lower bracket]"),
  tibble(cm = xs, d = dgamma(xs/100, shape = 2, rate = 2/mean(sim_cm$M))/100,
         curve = "Gamma(2)  [upper bracket]"))

ggplot() +
  geom_histogram(data = sim_cm, aes(cm, after_stat(density)), bins = 40,
                 fill = "grey80", colour = "grey55", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_line(data = curves, aes(cm, d, colour = curve, linetype = curve), linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("black", "firebrick", "royalblue3")) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "dashed", "dashed")) +
  labs(x = "donor-segment size (cM)", y = "density", colour = NULL, linetype = NULL,
       title = "Simulated cM segment lengths vs the fitted BC2S3 gamma",
       subtitle = sprintf("n=%d segments from the n=1500 BC2S3 sim | fitted gamma KS D=%.3f",
                          nrow(sim_cm), ks_gamma)) +
  theme(legend.position = c(0.72, 0.8), legend.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA))

Part 3 — cM-space validation of the five callers

Convert each caller’s called Mb segments back to cM by evaluating the consensus cumulative map at the segment endpoints and differencing, \(\Delta\text{cM}=M(\text{end\_bp})-M(\text{start\_bp})\) — a forward map lookup (per-chromosome monotone linear interpolation), no inversion. Then compare each caller’s cM distribution to the map-free reference: the BC2S3 expectation — the fitted \(\text{Gamma}(k,\lambda)\) whose family (not its \(k,\lambda\)) the Part 1 derivation fixes — and, equivalently, the simulation’s own cM lengths.

⚠ BrB-nilHMM caveat. BrB-nilHMM (the count HMM on the same BRB reads as BrB-RTI, BC2S3 freqs) is wired in as a co-equal caller, but on BRB it under-calls donor (genome fraction ~0.04 vs BrB-RTI’s ~0.17) and its KS-vs-sim rigidity rails to the grid edge, so its donor blocks are short/fragmented and its cM distribution sits well short of the BC2S3 Gamma by construction — expected, not a failure of the law. It also collapses ALT→HET (read its donor footprint, not its rates). Full diagnosis: agent/nilhmm/BRB_run_findings.md. Its segments are bp on B73 v5, so the same mb2cm consensus-map conversion applies as for every caller.

Code 
skim    <- read_csv(params$skim_calls, show_col_types = FALSE)
brb     <- read_csv(params$brb_taxa,   show_col_types = FALSE)
skimbin <- read_csv(params$skimbin,    show_col_types = FALSE)
nilhmm  <- read_csv(params$nilhmm,     show_col_types = FALSE)   # Skim-nilHMM, count-based caller, same skim reads
brbnil  <- read_csv(params$brbnil,     show_col_types = FALSE)   # BrB-nilHMM, count HMM on the SAME BRB reads as BrB-RTI (keyed on BRB name)
corr    <- read_csv(params$corr, show_col_types = FALSE) %>% filter(type == "NIL")

# scope = full set of NILs called on BOTH platforms (mirrors the Mb intro-size panel)
brb_in  <- corr %>% separate_rows(brbseq_prefix, sep = ";") %>%
  transmute(name = brbseq_prefix, nil = pedigree) %>% filter(name %in% brb$name)
skim_in <- corr %>% separate_rows(skim_prefix, sep = ";") %>%
  transmute(name = skim_prefix, nil = pedigree) %>% filter(name %in% skim$name)
both_nils <- intersect(brb_in$nil, skim_in$nil)

# consensus map -> per-chr monotone Mb->cM interpolator (dedup anchors that share a bp)
mp <- readRDS(params$map) %>% group_by(chr, bp) %>% summarise(cm = mean(cm), .groups = "drop")
mb2cm <- function(chr, bp) {
  out <- numeric(length(bp))
  for (cc in unique(chr)) {
    i <- chr == cc; a <- mp %>% filter(chr == cc) %>% arrange(bp)
    out[i] <- approx(a$bp, a$cm, xout = bp[i], rule = 2)$y   # rule=2 clamps endpoints past the last anchor
  }
  out
}

# donor block = maximal run of donor state (HET or ALT) within (sample, chromosome); size in cM
donor_blocks_cm <- function(seg) seg %>% arrange(name, chr, start_bp) %>% group_by(name, chr) %>%
  mutate(run = cumsum(c(TRUE, diff(state > 0) != 0)), donor = state > 0) %>% filter(donor) %>%
  group_by(name, chr, run) %>%
  summarise(s = min(start_bp), e = max(end_bp), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(cm = mb2cm(chr, e) - mb2cm(chr, s)) %>% filter(cm > 0)

skim_b <- donor_blocks_cm(skim    %>% filter(name %in% skim_in$name[skim_in$nil %in% both_nils])) %>% mutate(src = "Skim-RTI (r=5)")
brb_b  <- donor_blocks_cm(brb     %>% filter(name %in% brb_in$name [brb_in$nil  %in% both_nils])) %>% mutate(src = "BrB-RTI (r=7, ws)")
bin_b  <- donor_blocks_cm(skimbin %>% filter(name %in% skim_in$name[skim_in$nil %in% both_nils])) %>% mutate(src = "Skim-BIN (1 Mb)")
# Skim-nilHMM keyed on the skim sample name (same reads as Skim-RTI/Skim-BIN)
nil_b  <- donor_blocks_cm(nilhmm  %>% filter(name %in% skim_in$name[skim_in$nil %in% both_nils])) %>% mutate(src = "Skim-nilHMM (counts)")
# BrB-nilHMM keyed on the BRB sample name (same reads as BrB-RTI); same mb2cm conversion
brbnil_b <- donor_blocks_cm(brbnil %>% filter(name %in% brb_in$name[brb_in$nil %in% both_nils])) %>% mutate(src = "BrB-nilHMM (counts)")
called <- bind_rows(skim_b, brb_b, bin_b, nil_b, brbnil_b)

cat(sprintf("NILs on both platforms: %d | Skim-RTI %d | BrB-RTI %d | Skim-BIN %d | Skim-nilHMM %d | BrB-nilHMM %d blocks\n",
            length(both_nils), nrow(skim_b), nrow(brb_b), nrow(bin_b), nrow(nil_b), nrow(brbnil_b)))
NILs on both platforms: 332 | Skim-RTI 1909 | BrB-RTI 2747 | Skim-BIN 1782 | Skim-nilHMM 1825 | BrB-nilHMM 2569 blocks

  median_cM  = median(x),
  mean_cM    = mean(x),
  D_vs_Gamma = suppressWarnings(ks.test(x/100, "pgamma", shape = k, rate = lam)$statistic),
  D_vs_sim   = suppressWarnings(ks.test(x, sim_cm$cm)$statistic))

ks_summary <- called %>% group_by(src) %>% group_modify(~ ks_vs(.x$cm)) %>%
  mutate(across(c(median_cM, mean_cM), ~round(.,2)), across(starts_with("D_"), ~round(.,3)))

Code 
# On a log10 x-axis the histogram density is per-unit-log10(cM), so both references must be in
# that same space: the sim freqpoly is a ggplot stat (already in-space); the analytic gamma is a
# per-cM density and needs the change-of-variables Jacobian x*ln(10) to match the bars.
ggplot(called, aes(cm, fill = src)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), position = "identity", alpha = 0.45, bins = 30) +
  geom_freqpoly(data = sim_cm, aes(cm, after_stat(density)), bins = 30,
                colour = "grey25", linewidth = 0.8, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_line(data = curves %>% filter(grepl("BC2S3 expectation", curve)),
            aes(cm, d * cm * log(10)), colour = "black", linewidth = 0.9, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Skim-RTI (r=5)" = "purple4", "BrB-RTI (r=7, ws)" = "orange3",
                               "Skim-BIN (1 Mb)" = "seagreen4", "Skim-nilHMM (counts)" = "steelblue",
                               "BrB-nilHMM (counts)" = "navy")) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "donor-segment size (cM, log scale)", y = "density (per unit log10 cM)", fill = NULL,
       title = "Caller cM segment-size distributions vs the BC2S3 expectation",
       subtitle = "black = BC2S3 expectation (fitted Gamma, Jacobian-corrected for the log axis) | grey = n=1500 sim cM lengths") +
  theme(legend.position = c(0.01, 0.99), legend.justification = c("left", "top"),
        legend.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA))

Per-method gamma fits

Each caller’s own cM fragment-size distribution, with a gamma fit by MLE to that caller’s data (its own \(k,\lambda\) in the legend) — not the simulation-derived law. This reads off the effective shape and rate each method’s calls imply, and how well a gamma describes each.

Code 
fit_gamma <- function(x) {
  f <- suppressWarnings(MASS::fitdistr(x / 100, "gamma")$estimate)   # fit in Morgans
  tibble(k = unname(f["shape"]), lam = unname(f["rate"]))
}
fits <- called %>% group_by(src) %>% group_modify(~ fit_gamma(.x$cm)) %>% ungroup() %>%
  left_join(called %>% group_by(src) %>%
              summarise(xmax = quantile(cm, 0.99), mean_cm = mean(cm), .groups = "drop"),
            by = "src") %>%
  mutate(lab = sprintf("%s — Gamma(k=%.2f, λ=%.1f/M, mean %.0f cM)", src, k, lam, mean_cm))

mle_curves <- fits %>% group_by(src, lab) %>%
  reframe(cm = seq(0, xmax, length.out = 300), d = dgamma(cm / 100, k, lam) / 100)

src_col <- c("Skim-RTI (r=5)" = "purple4", "BrB-RTI (r=7, ws)" = "orange3",
             "Skim-BIN (1 Mb)" = "seagreen4", "Skim-nilHMM (counts)" = "steelblue",
             "BrB-nilHMM (counts)" = "navy")
pal_lab <- setNames(src_col[fits$src], fits$lab)

ggplot(called, aes(cm)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 30,
                 fill = "grey82", colour = "grey55", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_line(data = mle_curves, aes(cm, d, colour = lab), linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ src, ncol = 1, scales = "free") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal_lab, name = "MLE gamma fit (per method)") +
  labs(x = "donor-segment size (cM)", y = "density",
       title = "Per-method cM fragment-size distributions with their own MLE gamma fit") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(ncol = 1))

Each method’s own MLE gamma vs (i) its own data — does a gamma describe its shape at all — and (ii) the sim-derived benchmark gamma — how far its calls sit from the neutral model. The simulation row is the reference (its own gamma is the benchmark, so both KS columns equal its self-fit floor).

Code 
bench_k <- k; bench_lam <- lam   # sim-derived benchmark gamma (from Part 2)
fit_row <- function(x, label) {
  f <- suppressWarnings(MASS::fitdistr(x / 100, "gamma")$estimate)
  tibble(method = label, n = length(x),
         k = unname(f["shape"]), lambda = unname(f["rate"]), mean_cM = mean(x),
         D_own_gamma = suppressWarnings(ks.test(x/100, "pgamma", shape = f["shape"], rate = f["rate"])$statistic),
         D_vs_sim_gamma = suppressWarnings(ks.test(x/100, "pgamma", shape = bench_k, rate = bench_lam)$statistic))
}
ks_methods <- bind_rows(
  fit_row(sim_cm$cm, "Simulation (n=1500)"),
  called %>% group_split(src) %>%
    map_dfr(~ fit_row(.x$cm, .x$src[1]))) %>%
  mutate(across(c(k, lambda, mean_cM), ~round(., 2)),
         across(starts_with("D_"), ~round(., 3)))
knitr::kable(ks_methods,
  caption = "Per-method MLE gamma fit and KS distance, vs the method's own gamma and vs the sim-derived benchmark gamma (k=1.15, λ=4.72/Morgan).")

The Mb-space expectation is lognormal, not gamma

The clean gamma holds in cM. Pushed through the empirical, position-dependent genetic map (ρ(x) varies ~10× along the genome), the Mb fragment-size distribution becomes markedly more skewed (sim Mb CV 1.43, skew 2.08, vs the cM gamma’s 0.88, 1.57) and is best described by a lognormal, not a gamma — and there is no closed-form cM→Mb conversion (the position-mixture has no analytic form; this is why the derivation lives in cM). The table compares ways to express the BC2S3 expectation in Mb.

Code 
mb        <- nil_seg$mb[nil_seg$mb > 0]
genome_mb <- sum(read_csv("data/rtiger_50K/seqlengths.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)[[2]]) / 1e6
cm_tot    <- mp %>% group_by(chr) %>% summarise(L = max(cm), .groups = "drop") %>% pull(L) %>% sum()
rbar      <- cm_tot / genome_mb                      # genome-mean rate (cM/Mb)

mom      <- list(shape = mean(mb)^2 / var(mb), rate = mean(mb) / var(mb))
g_mb     <- suppressWarnings(MASS::fitdistr(mb, "gamma", start = mom)$estimate)
ln_mb    <- suppressWarnings(MASS::fitdistr(mb, "lognormal")$estimate)
lam_unif <- lam / 100 * rbar                         # cM gamma rate -> per-Mb under a uniform map

mk <- function(name, params, med, ks)
  tibble(`Mb representation` = name, params = params,
         `median Mb` = round(med, 1), `KS vs sim Mb` = round(ks, 3))
mb_tbl <- bind_rows(
  mk("(A) n=1500 sim Mb segments — the expectation", "empirical", median(mb), 0),
  mk("(A′) lognormal MLE", sprintf("μ=%.2f, σ=%.2f", ln_mb["meanlog"], ln_mb["sdlog"]),
     exp(ln_mb["meanlog"]), suppressWarnings(ks.test(mb, "plnorm", meanlog = ln_mb["meanlog"], sdlog = ln_mb["sdlog"])$statistic)),
  mk("(A″) gamma MLE", sprintf("k=%.2f, rate=%.3f/Mb", g_mb["shape"], g_mb["rate"]),
     qgamma(.5, g_mb["shape"], g_mb["rate"]), suppressWarnings(ks.test(mb, "pgamma", shape = g_mb["shape"], rate = g_mb["rate"])$statistic)),
  mk("(B) uniform-rate scaled cM gamma", sprintf("k=%.2f (same shape), rate=%.3f/Mb", k, lam_unif),
     qgamma(.5, k, lam_unif), suppressWarnings(ks.test(mb, "pgamma", shape = k, rate = lam_unif)$statistic)))
knitr::kable(mb_tbl, caption = sprintf(
  "BC2S3 expectation in Mb (genome %.0f Mb, map %.0f cM, mean rate %.2f cM/Mb). The cM gamma does NOT push forward to a gamma in Mb; lognormal fits best. (B) the naive uniform-rate scaling gets the mean right but the median/tail wrong.",
  genome_mb, cm_tot, rbar))
BC2S3 expectation in Mb (genome 2132 Mb, map 1783 cM, mean rate 0.84 cM/Mb). The cM gamma does NOT push forward to a gamma in Mb; lognormal fits best. (B) the naive uniform-rate scaling gets the mean right but the median/tail wrong.
Mb representation params median Mb KS vs sim Mb
(A) n=1500 sim Mb segments — the expectation empirical 10.8 0.000
(A′) lognormal MLE μ=2.31, σ=1.71 10.1 0.040
(A″) gamma MLE k=0.59, rate=0.021/Mb 15.0 0.084
(B) uniform-rate scaled cM gamma k=1.15 (same shape), rate=0.039/Mb 21.2 0.222

Convention. The n=1500 BC2S3 simulation (results/nil_segments.csv, mb column) is the BC2S3 expectation in Mb — use it directly as the reference (Null) in all Mb introgression-size plots. Do not substitute the uniform-rate-scaled gamma (row B: KS ≈ 0.22; right mean, wrong median/tail). The smooth parametric stand-in, if needed, is the lognormal (row A′), not a gamma. RTIGER rigidity (r) calibration targets this same distribution — the BrB-RTI KS sweep already does (ks_sweep_brbseq_wideseq.R keys on the mb column); Skim-RTI’s r=5 should be reconciled against the same reference.

Interpretation & caveats

  • The derivation is validated: the BC2S3 recombination model predicts a near-exponential gamma (\(k\gtrsim1\), \(\lambda\lesssim5\)/Morgan), and the simulation’s own cM lengths match it to KS \(D\approx0.028\) — so the BC2S3 expectation (the gamma family fixed by the derivation, with \(k,\lambda\) fitted to the sim) is a faithful, map-free stand-in for the n=1500 reference. (The derivation fixes the family + brackets + direction; \(k,\lambda\) are estimated, not closed-form.)
  • Caller comparison in cM (table above) mirrors the Mb panel but against the BC2S3 expectation. Deviations read the same way: a caller that over-fragments donor blocks shifts mass to short cM; one that under-resolves (Skim-BIN’s 1 Mb bins) loses the short tail.
  • Conserved marker order is load-bearing. The cM conversion uses the consensus \(\rho(x)\); for any introgression with local rearrangement the map is wrong and \(\Delta\)cM is biased. This assumption is heavier here than in the Mb panel.
  • Pericentromeric pile-up. Recombination deserts map large Mb spans to ≈0 cM, so a chunk of centromeric blocks collapse near cM 0 — map physics, not caller behavior.
  • Keep Mb for tuning r. The caller resolution limit is defined in Mb; cM smears it through the map. This panel is the validation view; the Mb panel remains the calibration space. Agreement across both is the robustness check.
